subject: Question about JAGS code in AHM2 book regarding joint occupancy models

messages.author: 5d8084b4d758276c
messages.subject: Question about JAGS code in AHM2 book regarding joint occupancy models
parts:
Hello everyone, hope you are all doing well. 

In CH2 in AHM2 book in the JAGS model for the joint occupancy model (Rota et al. 2019) there is a graph (Fig. 8.4) that has the predictions of all eight latent state probabilities as a function of covariate 1 while keeping covariate 2 constant at its mean. Part of the code to create that graph is pasted below. 

My question is why did the authors used cov2 for the joint species linear predictors (psiBC, etc.) and not cov1 all across all linear predictors?
If I had 3 covariates, for example, would I have to repeat lines 8-10 (psiBC,etc) with the other covariate to create this first graph?  


# Assemble the linear predictors

# ...for states B, C, and F

psiB <- as.numeric( psi_cov1 %*% tmp$betaB )

psiC <- as.numeric( psi_cov1 %*% tmp$betaC )

psiF <- as.numeric( psi_cov1 %*% tmp$betaF )



# ...for states BC, CF, and BF (in that order)

psiBC <- psiB + psiC + as.numeric( psi_cov2 %*% tmp$betaBC )

psiCF <- psiC + psiF + as.numeric( psi_cov2 %*% tmp$betaCF )

psiBF <- psiB + psiF + as.numeric( psi_cov2 %*% tmp$betaBF )



# ...for state ABC

psiBCF <- psiB + psiC + psiF + psiBC + psiCF + psiBF
​
Hope this makes sense and that I explained my question clearly. English is not my 1st language. 
Thank you in advance, 
Gabby

messages.author: 4f80e1927b0757cb
messages.subject: Re: Question about JAGS code in AHM2 book regarding joint occupancy models
parts:
Hi Gabby,

In the original description of the model (on page 473), the authors state that "...we fit an effect of Dist on the species main effects in occupancy, an effect of HDens on the two-way interactions in occupancy..."; thus when re-calculating the linear predictors from the JAGS output you have to use Dist for the main effects and HDens for the two- way interactions (and not the same covariate for both). I'm not sure this is quite what you are asking though. It might be helpful to look at the part of the actual JAGS code in which the linear predictors are calculated, on page 477. For example, a main effect:

psiB[i] <- inprod( betaB, psi_cov[i, ] )

and a two-way interaction

psiBC[i] <- inprod( betaBC, psi_inxs_cov[i, ] )

In this case, psi_cov in the JAGS code is equivalent to psi_cov1 in the plotting code, and psi_inxs_cov in the JAGS code is equivalent to psi_cov2 in the plotting code. Furthermore, psi_cov (= psi_cov1), associated with the main effects, is a model matrix containing a column of 1s for the intercept and a column of the Dist values, and psi_inxs_cov ( = psi_cov2), associated with the two-way interaction, is a model matrix containing a column of 1s for the intercept and a column of Hdens values. In the same way, betaB is a vector with a number of elements equal to the number of columns in psi_cov (2), and betaBC is a vector with a number of elements equal to the number of columns in psi_inxs_cov (2).

If you wanted to add a new additional covariate on the main effects you would (1) increase the length of betaB, C, and F from 2 to 3 (you would now have an intercept, an effect of Dist, and a new  covariate) which in the book code would mean changing the input data value for nfirst_order_psi to 3, and (2) add a new column to the model matrix psi_cov (and thus psi_cov1 in plotting code) containing your new covariate values. So the new model matrix would have 3 columns: intercept, Dist, and new covariate.

You would follow this same procedure with betaBC and psi_inxs_cov and psi_cov2 if you wanted to add a new covariate to the two-way interaction terms.

Ken
